clue.text: Bad temper shown when business is slack

parts.note: food that has gone bad is said to be off
to temper something is to moderate or flavour it, as to season it does

explanation.surface: Someone is in a foul mood because trade has dried up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad temper' reads as one phrase, a grumpy mood, but each word works alone: spoiled food, and the verb meaning to flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: The off-season is the quiet part of the year for a trade such as tourism, when few customers come.

clue.text: So Bunter would have done with too much cramming

definitions.text: So Bunter would have done with too much cramming

parts.words: So Bunter would have done with too much cramming
parts.note: Billy Bunter, the greedy fat schoolboy of British comic stories, stuffs himself with food, so too much cramming describes his habit at the tuck shop

explanation.surface: A comment on the famously greedy schoolboy Billy Bunter after a feast.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is a gluttonous schoolboy from Frank Richards's old British school stories. 'Cramming' hints at swotting for exams, but here it means stuffing in food.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has eaten far more than is good for them is described by this participle, which fits the stuffed schoolboy.

clue.text: Money initially needed for electric vehicle

definitions.meaning: the cash put in a till at the start of trading so change can be given
the milk delivery van of British streets, battery-powered

explanation.surface: Starting capital is needed to launch an electric car.
explanation.walkthrough: A milk float is the slow electric van British milkmen used for doorstep deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: A float is both the starting cash in a till and a battery-driven milk delivery van.

clue.text: Delicate English leather is fashionable

indicators.note: read as able to be fashioned, the letters before it are shaped into a new order

explanation.surface: Fine English leather is in vogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashionable' reads as 'in style', but here it means 'can be fashioned', which signals the anagram of E plus LEATHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ethereal is light, airy and otherworldly, so it can be called delicate.

clue.text: Traveller 'who died dramatically

parts.note: a commercial traveller whose death happens on stage, in Arthur Miller's play Death of a ...

explanation.surface: A travelling man meets a theatrical end.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Miller's play Death of a Salesman is about Willy Loman, a travelling sales rep. 'Dramatically' means 'in a play', not 'in a striking way'.
explanation.definitionFit: A commercial traveller is an old term for a sales rep who travels selling goods, like Willy Loman in Miller's drama.

clue.text: Mother perhaps unable 'to cope with a vacuum?

definitions.text: Mother perhaps unable 'to cope with a vacuum?

parts.words: Mother perhaps unable 'to cope with a vacuum?
parts.note: the proverb says the natural world abhors a vacuum, and the natural world is often called Mother, as in the phrase Mother ...

explanation.surface: A mum who can't manage the vacuum cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is a mother beaten by the housework. The real reference is the saying that nature abhors a vacuum, and 'Mother Nature'.
explanation.definitionFit: The physical world, personified as Mother, is said by the old proverb to abhor empty space.

clue.text: Locates speaker's spectacles

indicators.note: what a speaker says is heard rather than read, so the word for spectacles is taken by its pronunciation

parts.note: spectacles are sights, things worth seeing

explanation.surface: Someone finds the glasses belonging to a lecturer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spectacles' suggests glasses, but here it means sights, things to see.
explanation.definitionFit: To site something is to place or position it, so the verb is a synonym for locates.

clue.text: Security, say, involves festival 'ending prematurely

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap up or include, so the word say holds another piece inside it
the festival word stops one letter early, losing its last letter

parts.note: a fete is a village fair or festival

explanation.surface: Peace of mind at a festival that is cut short, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is used as written here, not as the usual signal for an example. 'Ending prematurely' drops the last letter of the festival word, and 'involves' wraps the result in the clue's own 'say'.
explanation.definitionFit: Safety and security are synonyms, both meaning freedom from danger.

clue.text: Exclusive hostelry linked with some public schoolboys

parts.note: things linked together are tied
British public (that is, private) schools split pupils into houses, so a house is a group of schoolboys

explanation.surface: A select inn has connections to boys from a posh school.
explanation.walkthrough: A tied house is a British pub bound to sell only one brewery's beer, hence 'exclusive'. British public schools are fee-paying and divide pupils into houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A tied house is a pub that may stock only its owning brewery's drinks, so it serves exclusively.

clue.text: Heavenly body captivates one in part of flight

indicators.note: to captivate is to capture and hold, so the star keeps the other letter inside

parts.note: a star is a heavenly body
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A celestial being charms someone on a plane journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' suggests air travel, but here it is a flight of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight of stairs is made up of single steps, each one part of the staircase.

clue.text: Old chapel, out of period

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: An old chapel that is not of its time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of period' reads as 'anachronistic', but 'out' is the anagram signal for O plus CHAPEL and 'of period' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Epochal means relating to an epoch, an era or historical period.

clue.text: Finish off product with a fine cheese cloth

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its end, so only the last letter is taken

parts.note: F stands for fine on pencil grades
feta is a Greek cheese

explanation.surface: A recipe step: top the dish with a good cheese, wrapped in muslin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheese cloth' looks like the muslin used in kitchens, but it splits: FETA ends the wordplay and 'cloth' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Taffeta is a crisp, lustrous woven fabric, often silk, used for dresses.

clue.text: Break into business without using force as a backup

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Break into business without using force as a backup (5)': ENTERPRISE less PRISE fits, but no reading makes 'using force as a backup' give PRISE, so the clue looks misread and no scan or search gives the printed text.
annotationWithheld.clue: Break into business without using force as a backup

clue.text: It's specifically carried in case of emergency

definitions.text: It's specifically carried in case of emergency

parts.words: It's specifically carried in case of emergency
parts.note: read as a kit item, it is something carried just in case; really it is the frame on which an injured person is carried by ambulance crews

explanation.surface: Something you pack just in case of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious reading is something you take with you for emergencies, like a first-aid kit. The twist is that it is the thing on which a casualty is carried.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretcher is a frame on which an injured or sick person is borne by two bearers.

clue.text: Vessel reconditioned in River Tamar

indicators.note: something reconditioned is rebuilt, so these letters are reassembled in a new order

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for river on maps
the Tamar is the river between Devon and Cornwall

explanation.surface: A boat that has been refitted is out on a Cornish river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tamar is the river dividing Devon from Cornwall in England.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimaran is a boat with three hulls side by side, a kind of sailing vessel.

clue.text: Diabolical jobs available for these unemployed workers

definitions.text: Diabolical jobs available for these unemployed workers

parts.words: Diabolical jobs available for these unemployed workers
parts.note: the proverb says the devil finds work for people who are doing nothing; the workers are body parts left idle

explanation.surface: Dreadful vacancies are on offer to people out of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diabolical' reads as 'awful', but it means 'from the devil', after the proverb 'the devil finds work for idle hands'. 'Workers' are hands, as in farmhands.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands is an everyday word for labourers, and idle ones have no work, as in the proverb.

clue.text: Girl's put off by deliberate swear-word

indicators.note: to put something off is to remove it, so the girl's name is taken away from the longer word

parts.note: to deliberate is to discuss
Di is a short girl's name, with the possessive giving DIS

explanation.surface: A girl is upset by a calculated oath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliberate' looks like an adjective, intentional, but it is the verb, discuss. 'Put off by' takes DI'S from DISCUSS.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuss is an oath or curse, a swear-word in informal American and British speech.

clue.text: Where to find spare part old 'car needed?

definitions.text: Where to find spare part old 'car needed?

parts.words: Where to find spare part old 'car needed?
parts.note: a breakers' yard where old cars are dumped is a place to hunt for spare parts, and it is also where an old car belongs

explanation.surface: A motorist asks where to get a part for an old car.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks where to buy a spare part. The answer is where old cars end up, and where an unneeded thing is thrown.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrapheap is a pile of discarded metal and old vehicles, where unwanted things are thrown away.

clue.text: Soldier -having a ball going round university for counselling

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so the soldier surrounds the next letter

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A soldier enjoying himself around campus gets advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having a ball' reads as 'enjoying himself', but 'a ball' is a formal party. 'Going round' wraps the soldier around the university letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Guidance means advice or direction, which is what counselling gives.

clue.text: Belgian subject

definitions.meaning: a man from the Belgian city of Liège
a vassal owing feudal service to a lord

explanation.surface: A Belgian citizen.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a split phrase, the answer is a man from Liège, Belgium; read whole, it is a feudal vassal.
explanation.definitionFit: A liegeman was a vassal sworn to serve a lord, so a subject; split, a Liège man is Belgian.

clue.text: Invalid showing no expression

definitions.meaning: blank or characterless, as in a face without feeling

explanation.surface: A sick person with a blank face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invalid' suggests a sick person, but it is the adjective, not valid.
explanation.definitionFit: Null means void in law, as in null and void, and also expressionless or blank.

clue.text: Christian could be one raising dissension on board

definitions.text: Christian could be one raising dissension on board

parts.words: Christian could be one raising dissension on board
parts.note: Fletcher Christian led the revolt on HMS Bounty, so he was a sailor who rose up against his captain

explanation.surface: A devout passenger stirs up trouble on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer, but it is Fletcher Christian, who led the 1789 mutiny on the Bounty.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutineer is a sailor or soldier who rebels against those in command, as Fletcher Christian did.

clue.text: Subject to, jostling in the snack bar

definitions.meaning: to batter or knock about repeatedly, as waves or wind do
a counter or café serving light refreshments, as at a railway station

explanation.surface: Being shoved about in a crowded café.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are said differently: BUFF-it for knocking about, BOO-fay for the snack bar.
explanation.definitionFit: To buffet is to strike repeatedly, and a buffet is also a counter serving food, as on a train.

clue.text: Stable 'showing signs, of interference

definitions.meaning: the crackle on a radio caused by electrical disturbance

explanation.surface: A steady thing showing evidence of meddling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interference' suggests meddling, but it is radio interference.
explanation.definitionFit: Static means unmoving, and also the crackling noise of electrical interference on a broadcast.

clue.text: All in here appearing worn out

definitions.meaning: used up, or tired to the point of collapse

explanation.surface: Everyone here looks tired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All in' looks like 'everyone present' alongside 'here', but it is a slang phrase for very tired.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhausted means drained of energy, the same as the slang phrase all in, and also used up.

clue.text: Fast days not all remember

indicators.note: only part of the word remember is used, so the answer sits inside it

explanation.surface: Not everyone recalls the days of fasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast days' seems a plain definition of something like Lent, but Ember days are the church's fasting days, four times a year.
explanation.definitionFit: Ember days are set days of fasting and prayer in the Western Christian calendar.

clue.text: Greek appearing for trial frames old gang

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so the outer pieces enclose the letter for old

parts.note: someone up before the magistrate is appearing in court

explanation.surface: A Greek in court is set up by an old criminal band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frames' plays on framing someone for a crime, but it is the container signal, and 'appearing for trial' means being up before the court.
explanation.definitionFit: A gang is a band of people acting together, and a group is likewise a set of people.

clue.text: Women's name in the dictionary is allowed

indicators.note: the letters for women and name are placed inside the dictionary's initials

parts.note: the OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
W is the abbreviation for women, as on toilet doors

explanation.surface: A women's name in the dictionary is permitted.
explanation.walkthrough: The OED, the Oxford English Dictionary, is 'the dictionary' in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To own a fault is to admit or concede it, so owned means admitted or allowed.

clue.text: It has been fine for a change — what a blessing!

indicators.note: a change alters the arrangement, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: F stands for fine on pencil grades

explanation.surface: Someone is glad the weather has turned fine at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It has been fine for a change' reads as relief about the weather. 'For a change' signals the anagram of IT, BEEN and F.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefit is an advantage or boon, which a blessing is too.

clue.text: One's put up with elections

parts.note: put up here means proposed as a candidate, not tolerated or given lodging, when elections come round

explanation.surface: Someone who has endured the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up with' reads as 'tolerated', but 'put up' means proposed as a candidate, and 'with elections' means at election time.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominee is a person proposed as a candidate for an office or award.

clue.text: One needing 'outside support to face further test

indicators.note: the single letter needs something on its outside, so the word for support is wrapped around it

parts.note: a rest is a support, as for a snooker cue
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A struggling student needs help before another exam.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is a student needing help. 'Needing outside' puts REST around I.
explanation.definitionFit: To resit is to take an examination again after failing it, so to face another test.

clue.text: Got rid of corruption and made a great profit

definitions.meaning: purged an organisation of graft or wrongdoing
slang for won or earned a lot of money

explanation.surface: A reformer who stamped out graft also got rich.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses use the same phrasal verb: to purge, and to make a fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: To clean up is to purge vice or dishonesty, and in slang to win big money.
